Tweet 1

A new paper from UIUC found that AI coding assistants fix more real bugs when the code around the model makes them trace, step by step, what a piece of code will do before they edit it, submit it, or test it.

Programmers call this desk checking: you walk through code with a sample input in your head, without running it. The authors named their version DeskCheck.

365 chars (over 280)

Tweet 2

Quick terms.

Coding assistant = an AI model that reads a code project, edits files and runs commands to fix a problem.
Harness = the code around the model: its instructions, its tools, and the order of its steps.
Patch = the edit that fixes the bug.
Test = a small program that runs the code and checks the answer.
Hidden test = a test the assistant never sees, used only for grading.
Token = a word or piece of a word. Models are billed by tokens.

449 chars (over 280)

Tweet 3

They started by reading 7,955 recorded attempts from six existing assistants on real GitHub bugs.

The models already trace code on their own in about two out of three attempts. Attempts with tracing fixed the bug 69.8% of the time, against 50.8% without. That shows the two go together, which is weaker than proof. And the tracing happens at random moments.

Here is a miss. Claude Code (Anthropic's coding assistant) read a bug report that hinted at code looping over settings. It tested the 7 helper functions that loop. The 8th helper crashes in a different way, and that is the one the hidden test checks.

610 chars (over 280)

Tweet 4

What DeskCheck does: it makes tracing a required part of five fixed steps. Each step runs as its own helper that starts with a clean slate, so notes from one step don't clutter the next.

1. Read the project. No edits allowed.
2. Find where to edit. Map which functions call which, pick likely paths, invent an input, trace it.
3. Write a fix, then trace the fix on sample inputs. If the result is wrong, revise.
4. List every requirement in the bug report and trace the fix against each one.
5. Write down unusual inputs and the answer each should give. Turn them into real tests and run them.

594 chars (over 280)

Tweet 5

Step 3 in action. The bug report says a function must raise an error when it is called from the parent process instead of a worker process. (A process is one running copy of a program.) The first fix raised the error in a different case.

A real test for this needs two running processes. The plain assistant spent 14 steps trying to set one up, gave up, and submitted the fix untested. It passed 2 of 5 hidden tests.

DeskCheck traced the fix by hand, saw the error would never be raised, and changed the condition. 5 of 5.

524 chars (over 280)

Tweet 6

The test: 731 real bugs from SWE-bench Pro, a public set in Python, Go, JavaScript and TypeScript. Hidden tests decide if a bug is fixed.

Same model, plain assistant vs DeskCheck built on top of it:

MiniMax-M3: 54.72% → 65.25%
GPT-5.6-Luna: 53.08% → 59.37%
Claude Haiku-4.5: 42.82% → 51.16%

That is about 6 to 11 more bugs fixed per 100, for 2 to 28 cents more per bug.

The first two compare against mini-SWE-Agent, a small open-source assistant. Claude Code has no official setup for this benchmark, so for the third the authors built a simple find, fix, test loop around it.

580 chars (over 280)

Tweet 7

Could the gain be luck? Models give different answers on each run.

They took the bugs only DeskCheck fixed (97, 49 and 74 per model) and ran the plain assistants twice more on them. The plain assistants fixed 16, 7 and 14 of those in at least one retry. Most of the gap held.

276 chars

Tweet 8

Which step matters most? They switched tracing on one step at a time, on 100 bugs with MiniMax-M3.

53% → 56% → 58% → 61% → 68%

The biggest jump came last, from the test step: listing inputs and expected answers before writing tests.

With tracing off everywhere, the five separate helpers scored 53%, the same as the plain assistant. So splitting the work into helpers added nothing by itself. The gain came from the tracing.

427 chars (over 280)

Tweet 9

What a better test looks like. The bug: a function that decides whether a store item is something other than a book. The plain assistant tested "DVD" and "paperback".

The hidden tests also tried lowercase "dvd" and a two-word item, "audio cassette". DeskCheck's list of inputs covered lowercase and two-word items, plus empty and missing inputs. It caught its own bug on the first run and fixed it.

399 chars (over 280)

Tweet 10

This builds on ExecCritic, a paper we covered in September. It found that weak tests make a fixer worse: 61.2% of bugs fixed with no tests, 57.3% with tests written by the same open model before training. Its answer was to train a separate test writer.

DeskCheck goes after the same weak spot with no training and the same model: make it write down inputs and expected answers before it writes the test.

Step 4 also echoes SpecGuard, where one AI reads only the task and writes down what the code must do. DeskCheck does that in a clean helper, then traces the fix against each requirement.

592 chars (over 280)

Tweet 11

Limits they say themselves. One benchmark, bug fixing only, and results may not carry over to other assistants or newer models. The one-step-at-a-time test used 100 bugs and one model.

The hidden tests also reject some correct fixes. People checked 234 bugs that both assistants failed and judged 94 and 96 of those fixes correct anyway. Most were in Go, where tests can call helper names that only the official fix uses. So small gaps between methods are shaky.

463 chars (over 280)

Tweet 12

What I still can't tell: how often the model's hand trace is actually right. A wrong trace that still leads to a good fix would look the same in these numbers. The authors list checking the traces as future work.

If you build coding assistants: before your assistant writes a test, have it write down the inputs and the answers it expects.
